title: Book 7 — Polymnia, Chapter 220
paragraphs: It is also reported, however, that Leonidas himself sent them away, out of concern that they should not perish, but thinking it unseemly for himself and for the Spartans present to abandon the post they had originally come to guard. I am inclined rather to this latter opinion: that because Leonidas perceived the allies were disheartened and unwilling to face the danger with him to the end, he ordered them to leave, while he held that for himself to depart was not honorable, whereas if he remained, great glory would be left behind him, and the prosperity of Sparta would not be blotted out. For the Pythian prophetess had given the Spartans an oracle, when they consulted her about this war at its outset, to the effect that either Lacedaemon must be destroyed by the barbarians, or their king must lose his life. The prophetess gave this answer in hexameter verses, which ran as follows:

“But as for you, you men who dwell in wide-spaced Sparta — either your glorious city is sacked by the sons of Perseus, or, if not, then a king of the Heraclean line, dead, shall be mourned by all within the borders of broad Lacedaemon. Him neither the might of bulls nor the raging of lions shall stop; for he has might like Zeus's; and I say he will not be restrained until he has utterly torn apart one or the other of these.”

I am of the opinion that Leonidas, considering these things and wanting to lay up glory for himself above all other Spartans, dismissed the allies — rather than that those who departed did so in such disorderly fashion because they were divided in opinion.
